title: When an oil shock can reach core inflation for several years
bank: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
summary: Oil can affect core inflation through two separate mechanisms. A larger share of the oil shock can reach non-energy prices, and each resulting increase in core inflation can take longer to fade. Andrea De Michelis, Musa Orak, Avani Pradhan and Albert Queralto find evidence for both changes after 2020 in a panel of five advanced economies. Their strongest specification produces a meaningful upside risk to inflation from elevated oil prices. They interpret its projections as an upper bound conditional on the post-pandemic relationships persisting. They observed little evidence of second-round effects from the latest shock at the time of writing. The projections are the authors’ research and carry no official forecast status.

The empirical exercise pools Canada, the euro area, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States from 2000 Q1 through 2026 Q2. It uses core PCE in the United States and core CPI elsewhere. Local-currency Brent price changes enter relative to core inflation, alongside lagged inflation, a national output gap and global supply-chain pressures. Pooling helps detect common changes in a short post-2020 sample, at the expense of some country-specific explanatory detail. The estimated rise in persistence is widespread. The rise in oil pass-through is significant for Canada, Japan and the United States, weaker and statistically uncertain for the euro area and the United Kingdom (empirical framework and footnotes 2–6).

Table 2 estimates that the sum of the two lagged core-inflation coefficients rose from about 0.35 to 0.65. A 10-percentage-point increase in relative oil-price inflation was previously associated with about 0.01 percentage point more core inflation, an estimate indistinguishable from zero. The corresponding post-pandemic estimate is 0.14 percentage point. In Figure 2 a different experiment, a permanent 10% rise in the oil price level, raises the core price level by about 0.35% after twelve quarters under the full specification, against about 0.05% under pre-pandemic dynamics. These are cumulative price-level effects. They do not imply an equivalent permanent addition to annual inflation. Much of the simulated increase builds over roughly eight quarters.

Figure 1 compares fitted four-quarter inflation across specifications. Allowing both coefficients to change reduces the post-2020 root-mean-squared error from 0.37 to 0.17 in Table 1. This is an in-sample improvement. Reopening demand, fiscal stimulus, labour-market tightness, supply bottlenecks and energy prices moved together during the estimation window. Observed oil changes incorporate demand as well as supply forces. The retrospective fit therefore does not identify the response to an isolated future oil shock.

Figure 3 makes the scenario’s dating especially important. It uses core inflation through 2026 Q2 and the Brent futures curve as of early August. The June supply-chain index starts 1.63 standard deviations above its historical mean and declines towards that mean. With both parameter changes, the unweighted five-economy average reaches nearly 2.8% around mid-2027 and falls towards 2.2% by end-2028. The specification with neither change peaks near 2.2%. Stronger pass-through amplifies the near-term rise; greater inertia sustains inflation after the energy impulse ebbs. The futures input is an oil price path and supplies no information about the market’s pricing of policy rates.

A structural simulation illustrates the policy trade-off (Figure 4). Reducing global oil supply raises production costs and weakens demand. With both higher persistence and stronger pass-through, the output hit is roughly twice that in the pre-pandemic calibration, yet the policy rule tightens more to contain inflation. A larger assumed oil share in production stands in for several possible channels through wages and intermediate costs. It illustrates a mechanism consistent with the regressions. It cannot establish which mechanism firms actually experienced or how any individual central bank would vote.

questions.question: Does stronger oil pass-through survive outside the exceptional reopening period?
questions.detail: The improvement in fit is substantial but the model also captures the coincidence of strong demand and supply disruptions. This distinction changes how much inflation protection an isolated energy shock warrants. Re-estimate with real-time forecast vintages, distinguish oil supply from demand disturbances, and compare the results with the earlier cross-country studies by Alp and colleagues and by De Michelis and colleagues cited in the note.

questions.question: Which economies warrant the largest adjustment to the inflation scenario?
questions.detail: Pooled results conceal a weaker oil coefficient in the euro area and the United Kingdom. A uniform change to policy-path assumptions across currencies could misstate relative rates risk. Check national core inflation baskets, local-currency energy costs and exposure to gas alongside disaggregated producer prices. Use official statistical releases and central-bank projections to test whether core components with high energy-input exposure move first.

questions.question: What observations would invalidate the upper-bound path before 2027?
questions.detail: The five-economy forecast depends on the early-August Brent curve, diminishing supply-chain stress and unchanged inflation parameters. The authors have not attributed current inflation readings to new second-round effects. Recreate the forecast using successive oil-curve vintages and the same published pressure index, then compare with observed underlying inflation and pricing intentions. Separate errors in the input paths from errors in the estimated propagation mechanism.
